units.title: Hello, COBOL!
units.summary: Write your first COBOL program, learn how its divisions fit together and print text with DISPLAY.

lesson.md: COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language) is one of the oldest programming languages. Banks, insurance companies and governments still run large COBOL programs every day. COBOL code reads almost like English sentences.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. HELLO.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    DISPLAY "Hello, COBOL!"
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: The first line, `>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE`, tells the compiler that you use **free format**: a line may start in any column. Older COBOL code uses fixed format, where some columns have special meanings. This course always uses free format.

`IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.` starts the first part of the program. `PROGRAM-ID. HELLO.` gives the program its name, here `HELLO`. `PROCEDURE DIVISION.` starts the part with the **statements**, the instructions that the computer runs from top to bottom.
`DISPLAY` prints text and then ends the line. Text in double quotes, like `"Hello, COBOL!"`, is a **literal**: COBOL prints it exactly as written. `STOP RUN` ends the program.

A COBOL program has up to four **divisions**, always in this order: `IDENTIFICATION`, `ENVIRONMENT`, `DATA` and `PROCEDURE`. Only the `IDENTIFICATION DIVISION` with `PROGRAM-ID` is required. You do not need the `ENVIRONMENT DIVISION` in this course, and you meet the `DATA DIVISION` in the next unit.
One `DISPLAY` can print several items. It puts them next to each other without spaces, so you add spaces inside the quotes yourself. Numbers like `42` need no quotes. Each `DISPLAY` prints one line.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. SHOW.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    DISPLAY "Total: " 42
    DISPLAY "A" "B" "C"
    DISPLAY "Done"
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: Add `WITH NO ADVANCING` to stay on the same line. The next `DISPLAY` then continues where the last one stopped.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. SAMELINE.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    DISPLAY "Loading" WITH NO ADVANCING
    DISPLAY "..." WITH NO ADVANCING
    DISPLAY " ready"
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: The period `.` ends every division header and the `PROGRAM-ID` line. In the `PROCEDURE DIVISION`, this course puts a period only after the last statement, `STOP RUN.`. COBOL ignores upper and lower case in keywords, so `display` works like `DISPLAY`, but most COBOL code is written in capitals.
In exercises, short examples often show only the statements of the `PROCEDURE DIVISION`. Imagine them inside a complete program like the ones above.

card: `>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE` lets lines start in any column
`IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.` + `PROGRAM-ID. NAME.` name the program
`PROCEDURE DIVISION.` holds the statements
`DISPLAY "Total: " 42` prints items side by side and ends the line
`STOP RUN.` ends the program

exercises.prompt: Which division holds the statements that the program runs?
exercises.explain: The statements, such as `DISPLAY` and `STOP RUN`, always go into the `PROCEDURE DIVISION`.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code: DISPLAY "A" "B" "C"
exercises.explain: `DISPLAY` prints its items next to each other without spaces and without the quotes.

exercises.prompt: How many lines does this print?
exercises.code:
DISPLAY "One" WITH NO ADVANCING
DISPLAY "Two"
DISPLAY "Three"
exercises.explain: `WITH NO ADVANCING` keeps `Two` on the same line as `One`. `Three` goes on the second line.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code: DISPLAY "Price: " 15 " EUR"
exercises.explain: The three items are printed side by side. The spaces come from inside the quotes.

exercises.statement: The `DATA DIVISION` may come before the `IDENTIFICATION DIVISION`.
exercises.explain: The divisions always come in the same order, and `IDENTIFICATION DIVISION` is first.
COBOL ignores upper and lower case in keywords. Only the text inside quotes is printed exactly as written.

exercises.prompt: Complete the program so it prints Hello.
exercises.code:
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. HELLO.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    ___ "Hello"
    STOP RUN.
exercises.explain: COBOL prints with `DISPLAY`. `WRITE` exists, but it writes to files.

exercises.prompt: Complete the line that ends the program.
exercises.code:
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. BYE.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    DISPLAY "Bye"
    ___ RUN.
exercises.explain: `STOP RUN` ends a COBOL program.

exercises.prompt: Build the statement that prints Hi and stays on the same line.
exercises.explain: `WITH NO ADVANCING` comes after the items, so the line does not end.

exercises.prompt: Put the lines in order to make a complete program that prints Ready.
exercises.explain: First the `IDENTIFICATION DIVISION` with the `PROGRAM-ID`, then the `PROCEDURE DIVISION` with the statements. `STOP RUN` comes last.

exercises.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
Which line has the bug?
exercises.explain: A division header ends with a period. Write `PROCEDURE DIVISION.`.

units.title: Data and PIC clauses
units.summary: Declare data items in WORKING-STORAGE, describe them with PIC clauses, give them start values and copy data with MOVE.

lesson.md: A program keeps values in **data items**, which other languages call variables. In COBOL you declare every data item before you use it. Data items go into the `DATA DIVISION`, in the `WORKING-STORAGE SECTION`, between the `IDENTIFICATION DIVISION` and the `PROCEDURE DIVISION`.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. CITIES.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 CITY PIC X(5) VALUE "Paris".
01 FOUNDED PIC 9(4) VALUE 1190.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    DISPLAY "City: " CITY
    DISPLAY "Founded: " FOUNDED
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: Each declaration is one line that ends with a period. `01` is the **level number**: `01` means a data item of its own. Then comes the name, which may use letters, digits and hyphens. `PIC` (short for picture) describes what the item can hold, and `VALUE` gives it a start value.

In a `PIC` clause, `9` stands for one digit, `X` for any character and `A` for a letter or a space. A number in parentheses repeats the character: `9(4)` is the same as `9999`, and `X(5)` holds exactly five characters.

The size is fixed. A number always shows all its digits, so `PIC 9(3)` with the value `7` prints `007`. Text that is shorter than its item is filled with spaces on the right. The brackets in the next example only show where the item starts and ends.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. SIZES.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 SCORE PIC 9(3) VALUE 7.
01 TOWN PIC X(6) VALUE "Rome".
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    DISPLAY SCORE
    DISPLAY "[" TOWN "]"
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: `MOVE 25 TO AGE` puts `25` into `AGE` and replaces the old value. `MOVE OLD-AGE TO AGE` copies the value of `OLD-AGE` into `AGE`, and `OLD-AGE` keeps its value. One `MOVE` can fill several items: `MOVE 0 TO A B`.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. MOVES.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 AGE PIC 99 VALUE 18.
01 OLD-AGE PIC 99.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    DISPLAY AGE
    MOVE 25 TO AGE
    DISPLAY AGE
    MOVE AGE TO OLD-AGE
    MOVE 30 TO AGE
    DISPLAY OLD-AGE " " AGE
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: When a value is too big for its item, COBOL cuts it off without an error. Text loses characters on the **right**. Numbers lose digits on the **left**, because COBOL keeps the digits that line up with the item.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. CUTS.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 SHORT-NAME PIC X(4).
01 NUM PIC 99.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    MOVE "Alexander" TO SHORT-NAME
    MOVE 1234 TO NUM
    DISPLAY SHORT-NAME
    DISPLAY NUM
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: Higher level numbers such as `05` build a **group**: the `05` items belong to the `01` item above them. The group is all of its items in a row, so `DISPLAY PERSON` prints both parts without a space. A group has no `PIC` of its own.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. GROUPS.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 PERSON.
    05 FIRST-NAME PIC X(3) VALUE "Ana".
    05 BIRTH-YEAR PIC 9(4) VALUE 1990.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    DISPLAY FIRST-NAME
    DISPLAY PERSON
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: From now on, short examples in exercises show the data items and the statements together. Imagine the `01` lines in the `WORKING-STORAGE SECTION` and the statements in the `PROCEDURE DIVISION`, followed by `STOP RUN`.

card: `WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.` lists the data items
`01 AGE PIC 99 VALUE 18.` = level, name, picture, start value
`9` digit, `X` any character, `A` letter; `X(5)` = `XXXXX`
`MOVE 25 TO AGE` replaces the value
Too big: text is cut on the right, numbers on the left

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
01 SCORE PIC 9(4) VALUE 42.
DISPLAY SCORE
exercises.explain: `PIC 9(4)` always shows four digits, so COBOL adds two zeros on the left.

exercises.prompt: Which picture can hold the name Maria?
exercises.explain: `X` holds any character and `X(10)` has room for ten of them. `PIC X` holds only one character, and `9` is meant only for digits.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
01 TOWN PIC X(5).
MOVE "Barcelona" TO TOWN
DISPLAY TOWN
exercises.explain: `TOWN` has room for five characters. Text is cut off on the right.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
01 YY PIC 99.
MOVE 2025 TO YY
DISPLAY YY
exercises.explain: `YY` has two digits. Numbers lose their digits on the left, so `25` stays.

exercises.statement: `PIC 9(3)` and `PIC 999` describe the same kind of data item.
exercises.explain: The number in parentheses repeats the character, so `9(3)` means three digits, like `999`.

exercises.prompt: Complete the declaration so that AGE starts at 30.
exercises.code:
01 AGE PIC 99 ___ 30.
DISPLAY AGE
exercises.explain: `VALUE` gives a data item its start value.

exercises.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 5.
exercises.code:
01 QTY PIC 9.
___ 5 TO QTY
DISPLAY QTY
exercises.explain: `MOVE 5 TO QTY` puts the value `5` into `QTY`.

exercises.prompt: Build the statement that copies PRICE into OLD-PRICE.
exercises.explain: `MOVE` names the source first and the target after `TO`.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
01 ITEM-CODE.
    05 LETTERS PIC X(3) VALUE "ABC".
    05 DIGITS PIC 99 VALUE 7.
DISPLAY ITEM-CODE
exercises.explain: A group is all of its items in a row. `DIGITS` has two digits, so `7` prints as `07`.

exercises.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
Which line has the bug?
exercises.explain: `MOVE` always uses `TO`. Write `MOVE "Rome" TO TOWN`.

exercises.prompt: Which line has the bug?
exercises.explain: `PIC 99` holds at most `99`, so the start value `100` does not fit. Use `PIC 999`.

units.title: Arithmetic
units.summary: Calculate with ADD, SUBTRACT, MULTIPLY, DIVIDE and COMPUTE, and work with decimals and ROUNDED.

lesson.md: COBOL has an English verb for each kind of calculation. `ADD 5 TO TOTAL` adds `5` to `TOTAL` and stores the result in `TOTAL`. `SUBTRACT 3 FROM TOTAL` subtracts. `MULTIPLY 2 BY TOTAL` and `DIVIDE 4 INTO TOTAL` also store their result in `TOTAL`, the last item.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. VERBS.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 TOTAL PIC 999 VALUE 10.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    ADD 5 TO TOTAL
    DISPLAY TOTAL
    SUBTRACT 3 FROM TOTAL
    DISPLAY TOTAL
    MULTIPLY 2 BY TOTAL
    DISPLAY TOTAL
    DIVIDE 4 INTO TOTAL
    DISPLAY TOTAL
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: With `GIVING`, the result goes into another item and the inputs stay the same. `DIVIDE A BY B GIVING C` divides `A` by `B`. Add `REMAINDER R` to keep what is left over.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. GIVING.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 A PIC 99 VALUE 17.
01 B PIC 99 VALUE 5.
01 C PIC 99.
01 R PIC 99.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    ADD A TO B GIVING C
    DISPLAY "Sum: " C
    MULTIPLY A BY B GIVING C
    DISPLAY "Product: " C
    DIVIDE A BY B GIVING C REMAINDER R
    DISPLAY "Quotient: " C " Remainder: " R
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: `COMPUTE` calculates a whole formula and stores the result in the item before `=`. It uses `+` and `-`, `*` to multiply, `/` to divide and `**` for a power. `*` and `/` come before `+` and `-`, and parentheses change the order.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. FORMULA.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 RESULT PIC 999.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    COMPUTE RESULT = 2 + 3 * 4
    DISPLAY RESULT
    COMPUTE RESULT = (2 + 3) * 4
    DISPLAY RESULT
    COMPUTE RESULT = 2 ** 5
    DISPLAY RESULT
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: Always put spaces around the operators. A hyphen can be part of a name, so COBOL reads `A-B` as one name, not as `A` minus `B`. Write `A - B`.

`V` in a picture marks where the decimal point is. `PIC 9(3)V99` holds three digits before the point and two after it. The point is not stored, so to print the number nicely you move it to an **edited** picture. In an edited picture, `.` prints the point and `Z` prints a space instead of a leading zero.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. PRICE.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 PRICE PIC 9(3)V99 VALUE 4.25.
01 SHOWN PIC ZZ9.99.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    MULTIPLY 3 BY PRICE
    MOVE PRICE TO SHOWN
    DISPLAY "Total:" SHOWN
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: If a result has more decimals than the item can hold, COBOL cuts the extra digits off. Add `ROUNDED` after the result item to round instead: `2.5` becomes `3`.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. ROUND.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 WHOLE PIC 99.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    COMPUTE WHOLE = 10 / 4
    DISPLAY WHOLE
    COMPUTE WHOLE ROUNDED = 10 / 4
    DISPLAY WHOLE
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: A result that is too big loses its digits on the left without an error: `99 + 1` in `PIC 99` gives `00`. Add `ON SIZE ERROR` and a statement to react instead, for example `ADD 1 TO N ON SIZE ERROR DISPLAY "Too big" END-ADD`. Then `N` keeps its old value.

card: `ADD 5 TO N`, `SUBTRACT 3 FROM N`, `MULTIPLY 2 BY N`, `DIVIDE 4 INTO N`
`DIVIDE A BY B GIVING C REMAINDER R`
`COMPUTE C = (A + B) * 2 ** 3` with spaces around operators
`PIC 9(3)V99` stores decimals; `PIC ZZ9.99` prints them
`COMPUTE N ROUNDED = 10 / 4` rounds instead of cutting

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
01 N PIC 99 VALUE 7.
ADD 5 TO N
DISPLAY N
exercises.explain: `ADD 5 TO N` adds `5` to `7` and stores `12` in `N`.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
01 Q PIC 9.
01 R PIC 9.
DIVIDE 17 BY 5 GIVING Q REMAINDER R
DISPLAY "Q=" Q " R=" R
exercises.explain: `17` divided by `5` is `3`, and `2` is left over.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
01 N PIC 99 VALUE 4.
MULTIPLY 3 BY N
DISPLAY N
exercises.explain: Without `GIVING`, `MULTIPLY 3 BY N` stores the result `12` in `N`.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
01 X PIC 99.
COMPUTE X = 2 + 3 * 4
DISPLAY X
exercises.explain: `*` comes before `+`: `3 * 4` is `12`, plus `2` is `14`.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
01 Y PIC 9.
COMPUTE Y ROUNDED = 7 / 2
DISPLAY Y
exercises.explain: `7 / 2` is `3.5`. `Y` has no decimals, and `ROUNDED` rounds `3.5` up to `4`. Without `ROUNDED`, you get `3`.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
01 SHOWN PIC ZZ9.
MOVE 7 TO SHOWN
DISPLAY "[" SHOWN "]"
exercises.explain: Each `Z` prints a space instead of a leading zero. The item still has three characters.

exercises.statement: This program stops with an error because the result does not fit.
exercises.code:
01 N PIC 99 VALUE 1.
ADD 99 TO N
DISPLAY N
exercises.explain: COBOL cuts the result `100` to the two digits `00` and goes on. Use `ON SIZE ERROR` to notice it.

exercises.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 12.
exercises.code:
01 PRICE PIC 9 VALUE 3.
01 QTY PIC 9 VALUE 4.
01 TOTAL PIC 99.
MULTIPLY PRICE BY QTY ___ TOTAL
DISPLAY TOTAL
exercises.explain: `GIVING TOTAL` stores the result in `TOTAL` and leaves `PRICE` and `QTY` as they are.

exercises.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 025, the square of SIDE.
exercises.code:
01 SIDE PIC 99 VALUE 5.
01 SQ PIC 999.
COMPUTE SQ = SIDE ___ 2
DISPLAY SQ
exercises.explain: `**` is the power operator: `5 ** 2` is `25`. `SIDE * 2` would give `10`.

exercises.prompt: Build the statement that subtracts 4 from TOTAL.
exercises.explain: `SUBTRACT` names the amount first and the item after `FROM`.

exercises.prompt: Which line has the bug?
exercises.explain: COBOL reads `A-B` as one name. Put spaces around the minus: `COMPUTE C = A - B`.

exercises.prompt: Match each statement with what it does to N.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Let the program choose with IF, ELSE and EVALUATE, and give values readable names with level 88.

lesson.md: `IF` runs statements only when a condition is true. `ELSE` adds statements for the other case, and `END-IF` closes the `IF`. Indent the statements inside so that you can see what belongs together.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. ADULT.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 AGE PIC 99 VALUE 15.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    IF AGE >= 18
        DISPLAY "Adult"
    ELSE
        DISPLAY "Young"
    END-IF
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: You can compare with `=`, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=` and `NOT =` (not equal). COBOL also accepts words, such as `IS GREATER THAN` and `IS EQUAL TO`. `AND` needs both conditions to be true, `OR` needs at least one, and `NOT` turns a condition around.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. RANGE.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 TEMP PIC 99 VALUE 20.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    IF TEMP > 15 AND TEMP < 25
        DISPLAY "Pleasant"
    END-IF
    IF TEMP IS GREATER THAN 30 OR TEMP IS LESS THAN 0
        DISPLAY "Extreme"
    ELSE
        DISPLAY "Normal"
    END-IF
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: Do not put a period inside an `IF`. A period ends the whole sentence, so it also ends the `IF`, and the next `ELSE` becomes an error. Close every `IF` with `END-IF` instead.

`EVALUATE` compares one item with several values. Each `WHEN` names a value, and `WHEN OTHER` catches everything else. COBOL runs only the first `WHEN` that matches and then continues after `END-EVALUATE`.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. WEEKDAY.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 DAY-NUM PIC 9 VALUE 4.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    EVALUATE DAY-NUM
        WHEN 1
            DISPLAY "Monday"
        WHEN 2
            DISPLAY "Tuesday"
        WHEN 3 THRU 5
            DISPLAY "Midweek"
        WHEN OTHER
            DISPLAY "Weekend"
    END-EVALUATE
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: `WHEN 3 THRU 5` matches every value from `3` to `5`. With `EVALUATE TRUE`, each `WHEN` holds a full condition, and the first true one wins.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. GRADES.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 POINTS PIC 999 VALUE 72.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    EVALUATE TRUE
        WHEN POINTS >= 90
            DISPLAY "Excellent"
        WHEN POINTS >= 50
            DISPLAY "Passed"
        WHEN OTHER
            DISPLAY "Failed"
    END-EVALUATE
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: A level `88` item gives a value of the item above it a name. With `88 IS-RED VALUE "R"`, the condition `IF IS-RED` means `IF LIGHT = "R"`. `SET IS-GREEN TO TRUE` moves the value of `IS-GREEN` into `LIGHT`. A level `88` item can also list several values or a range with `THRU`.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. LIGHTS.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 LIGHT PIC X VALUE "R".
    88 IS-RED VALUE "R".
    88 IS-GREEN VALUE "G".
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    IF IS-RED
        DISPLAY "Stop"
    END-IF
    SET IS-GREEN TO TRUE
    DISPLAY LIGHT
    IF NOT IS-RED
        DISPLAY "Go"
    END-IF
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: Condition names make code easier to read: `IF IS-WEEKEND` explains itself, `IF DAY-NUM > 5` does not. Use them for values that have a meaning in your program.

card: `IF A > B ... ELSE ... END-IF`, no period inside
`EVALUATE X WHEN 1 ... WHEN 2 THRU 5 ... WHEN OTHER ... END-EVALUATE`
`EVALUATE TRUE` + `WHEN condition`: the first true one wins
`88 IS-RED VALUE "R".` then `IF IS-RED`, `SET IS-RED TO TRUE`

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
01 AGE PIC 99 VALUE 15.
IF AGE >= 18
    DISPLAY "Adult"
ELSE
    DISPLAY "Young"
END-IF
exercises.explain: `15` is not `>=` `18`, so the `ELSE` part runs.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
01 N PIC 9 VALUE 5.
IF N > 3 AND N < 5
    DISPLAY "A"
ELSE
    DISPLAY "B"
END-IF
exercises.explain: `N < 5` is false for `5`. With `AND`, both conditions must be true, so the `ELSE` part runs.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
01 N PIC 9 VALUE 7.
EVALUATE TRUE
    WHEN N > 5
        DISPLAY "Big"
    WHEN N > 0
        DISPLAY "Positive"
    WHEN OTHER
        DISPLAY "Zero"
END-EVALUATE
exercises.explain: Both conditions are true, but `EVALUATE` runs only the first `WHEN` that matches.

exercises.statement: When several `WHEN` branches of an `EVALUATE` match, all of them run.
exercises.explain: Only the first matching `WHEN` runs. Then the program continues after `END-EVALUATE`.

exercises.prompt: Complete the condition so the code prints Not ten.
exercises.code:
01 N PIC 99 VALUE 5.
IF N ___ 10
    DISPLAY "Not ten"
END-IF
exercises.explain: COBOL writes not equal as `NOT =`. The operator `!=` from other languages does not exist in COBOL.

exercises.prompt: Complete the code so it compiles and prints Even.
exercises.code:
01 N PIC 9 VALUE 4.
01 HALF PIC 9.
01 REST PIC 9.
DIVIDE N BY 2 GIVING HALF REMAINDER REST
IF REST = 0
    DISPLAY "Even"
___
exercises.explain: `END-IF` closes an `IF`. COBOL writes it with a hyphen.

exercises.prompt: Build the statement that prints Big when TOTAL is greater than 100.
exercises.explain: The condition comes after `IF`, then the statement, and `END-IF` closes it.

exercises.prompt: Put the lines in order so the code prints Positive when N is 3.
exercises.explain: The condition comes first, then the statements for true, `ELSE`, the statements for false, and `END-IF`.

exercises.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
Which line has the bug?
exercises.explain: You set a condition name with `TRUE`: `SET IS-GREEN TO TRUE`. COBOL then moves `"G"` into `LIGHT`.

exercises.prompt: Which line has the bug?
exercises.explain: The period ends the `IF` too early, so `ELSE` has no `IF` any more. Remove the period: `DISPLAY "Big"`.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:
01 SCORE PIC 99 VALUE 75.
    88 PASSED VALUE 50 THRU 99.
IF PASSED
    DISPLAY "Pass"
ELSE
    DISPLAY "Fail"
END-IF
exercises.explain: `75` is between `50` and `99`, so the condition name `PASSED` is true.

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat statements with PERFORM TIMES, count with PERFORM VARYING and loop until a condition is true with PERFORM UNTIL.

lesson.md: `PERFORM` repeats statements. `PERFORM 3 TIMES` runs the statements up to `END-PERFORM` three times. Instead of a number you can also use a data item, for example `PERFORM ROUNDS TIMES`.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. REPEAT.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    PERFORM 3 TIMES
        DISPLAY "Hello"
    END-PERFORM
    DISPLAY "Done"
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: `PERFORM VARYING I FROM 1 BY 1 UNTIL I > 5` uses `I` as a counter. It sets `I` to `1`, checks the condition before each round and adds `1` after each round. The loop stops as soon as the condition after `UNTIL` is true.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. COUNTING.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 I PIC 9.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    PERFORM VARYING I FROM 1 BY 1 UNTIL I > 5
        DISPLAY I WITH NO ADVANCING
    END-PERFORM
    DISPLAY " end"
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: `BY` sets the step. Here the loop adds the even numbers from `2` to `10`. A loop like this often builds a result, such as a total, in another data item.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. EVENS.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 N PIC 99.
01 TOTAL PIC 999 VALUE 0.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    PERFORM VARYING N FROM 2 BY 2 UNTIL N > 10
        ADD N TO TOTAL
    END-PERFORM
    DISPLAY "Total: " TOTAL
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: After the loop, the counter keeps the value that stopped it. After `UNTIL I > 5` with step `1`, `I` is `6`.

`PERFORM UNTIL` repeats until a condition becomes true. It checks the condition **before** each round, so the body may not run at all. Make sure that the statements inside change something, or the loop never ends.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. DOUBLE.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 AMOUNT PIC 999 VALUE 1.
01 STEPS PIC 9 VALUE 0.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    PERFORM UNTIL AMOUNT > 100
        MULTIPLY 2 BY AMOUNT
        ADD 1 TO STEPS
    END-PERFORM
    DISPLAY AMOUNT " after " STEPS " steps"
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: With `WITH TEST AFTER`, COBOL checks the condition after each round instead. The body then always runs at least once.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. TESTAFTER.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 N PIC 9 VALUE 5.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    PERFORM WITH TEST AFTER UNTIL N > 3
        DISPLAY "Round " N
        ADD 1 TO N
    END-PERFORM
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: A counter needs enough digits. `PIC 9` holds at most `9`, so `9 + 1` becomes `0`, and `UNTIL I > 9` is never true. The loop then runs forever. Use `PIC 99` for a counter that must reach `10`.

card: `PERFORM 3 TIMES ... END-PERFORM`
`PERFORM VARYING I FROM 1 BY 1 UNTIL I > 5 ... END-PERFORM`
`PERFORM UNTIL X > 100 ... END-PERFORM` checks before each round
`WITH TEST AFTER` checks after each round
Give the counter enough digits, or the loop never ends

units.title: Paragraphs
units.summary: Split the PROCEDURE DIVISION into named paragraphs and run them with PERFORM.

lesson.md: Long programs are hard to read. A **paragraph** is a named group of statements in the `PROCEDURE DIVISION`. Its name stands on its own line and ends with a period. The paragraph ends with a period after its last statement.

`PERFORM GREET` runs the paragraph `GREET` and then comes back to the next statement. The first paragraph is the main part of the program, often called `MAIN-PARA`. It ends with `STOP RUN`, so the program does not run into the paragraphs below it.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. PARAS.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
MAIN-PARA.
    DISPLAY "Start"
    PERFORM GREET
    PERFORM GREET
    DISPLAY "End"
    STOP RUN.

GREET.
    DISPLAY "Hello".

lesson.md: All paragraphs use the same data items from `WORKING-STORAGE`. To give a paragraph input, move values into data items before the `PERFORM`. The paragraph leaves its result in a data item, too.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. SQUARES.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 N PIC 9.
01 RESULT PIC 99.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
MAIN-PARA.
    MOVE 4 TO N
    PERFORM CALC-SQUARE
    DISPLAY N " squared is " RESULT
    MOVE 7 TO N
    PERFORM CALC-SQUARE
    DISPLAY N " squared is " RESULT
    STOP RUN.

CALC-SQUARE.
    COMPUTE RESULT = N * N.

lesson.md: All forms of `PERFORM` from the last unit also work with a paragraph name. `PERFORM SHOW-LINE 3 TIMES` runs the paragraph three times. `PERFORM SHOW-ROW VARYING R FROM 1 BY 1 UNTIL R > 3` runs it once for each value of `R`. These forms have no `END-PERFORM`.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. ROWS.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 R PIC 9.
01 TRIPLE PIC 9.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
MAIN-PARA.
    PERFORM SHOW-ROW VARYING R FROM 1 BY 1 UNTIL R > 3
    STOP RUN.

SHOW-ROW.
    COMPUTE TRIPLE = R * 3
    DISPLAY R " x 3 = " TRIPLE.

lesson.md: Without `STOP RUN`, the program does not stop at the end of the main paragraph. It goes on with the next paragraph, so that paragraph runs one extra time.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. NOSTOP.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
MAIN-PARA.
    PERFORM SAY-HI
    DISPLAY "Bye".

SAY-HI.
    DISPLAY "Hi".

lesson.md: `PERFORM STEP-1 THRU STEP-3` runs all paragraphs from `STEP-1` to `STEP-3` in the order in which they appear in the code, and then comes back.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. THRU.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
MAIN-PARA.
    PERFORM STEP-1 THRU STEP-3
    STOP RUN.

STEP-1.
    DISPLAY "Wash".

STEP-2.
    DISPLAY "Cut".

STEP-3.
    DISPLAY "Cook".

lesson.md: Give each paragraph one clear task and a name that says what it does, such as `PRINT-TOTAL` or `READ-NEXT`. Then `MAIN-PARA` reads like a table of contents.

card: `NAME.` on its own line starts a paragraph; a period ends it
`PERFORM NAME` runs it and comes back
`PERFORM NAME 3 TIMES`, `PERFORM NAME VARYING ... UNTIL ...`
`PERFORM A THRU C` runs A to C in order
End the main paragraph with `STOP RUN.`

units.title: Tables
units.summary: Store many values under one name with OCCURS, reach them with subscripts and process them in loops.

lesson.md: A **table** holds many values of the same kind under one name. Other languages call it an array. You create one with `OCCURS`: `05 TEMP PIC 99 OCCURS 3 TIMES` makes three items called `TEMP`. Put the table inside a group item, here `TEMPS`, so that you can also use all elements together.
A **subscript** in parentheses picks one element: `TEMP(1)` is the first, `TEMP(3)` the last. COBOL starts counting at `1`, not at `0`.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. TEMPS.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 TEMPS.
    05 TEMP PIC 99 OCCURS 3 TIMES.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    MOVE 12 TO TEMP(1)
    MOVE 15 TO TEMP(2)
    MOVE 9 TO TEMP(3)
    DISPLAY "Second day: " TEMP(2)
    DISPLAY "All: " TEMPS
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: The subscript can also be a data item, such as `TEMP(I)`. Together with `PERFORM VARYING`, this lets one loop visit every element.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. SQUARES.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 SQUARES.
    05 SQ PIC 99 OCCURS 5 TIMES.
01 I PIC 9.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    PERFORM VARYING I FROM 1 BY 1 UNTIL I > 5
        COMPUTE SQ(I) = I * I
    END-PERFORM
    PERFORM VARYING I FROM 1 BY 1 UNTIL I > 5
        DISPLAY SQ(I) WITH NO ADVANCING
        DISPLAY " " WITH NO ADVANCING
    END-PERFORM
    DISPLAY "end"
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: A group with a table can get a `VALUE` with all elements written one after another. Here `"254012"` fills three prices with two digits each: `25`, `40` and `12`. A loop then adds them up and finds the largest one.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. PRICES.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 PRICES VALUE "254012".
    05 PRICE PIC 99 OCCURS 3 TIMES.
01 I PIC 9.
01 TOTAL PIC 999 VALUE 0.
01 BIGGEST PIC 99 VALUE 0.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    PERFORM VARYING I FROM 1 BY 1 UNTIL I > 3
        ADD PRICE(I) TO TOTAL
        IF PRICE(I) > BIGGEST
            MOVE PRICE(I) TO BIGGEST
        END-IF
    END-PERFORM
    DISPLAY "Total: " TOTAL
    DISPLAY "Biggest: " BIGGEST
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: `INITIALIZE` resets a whole table at once: number items become zero and text items become spaces.
`OCCURS` also works on a group. Each element then has several parts. `FRUIT-NAME(2)` is the name in the second element, and `FRUIT-QTY(2)` is its quantity.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. STOCK.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 STOCK.
    05 FRUIT OCCURS 2 TIMES.
        10 FRUIT-NAME PIC X(6).
        10 FRUIT-QTY PIC 99.
01 I PIC 9.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    MOVE "Apple" TO FRUIT-NAME(1)
    MOVE 12 TO FRUIT-QTY(1)
    MOVE "Pear" TO FRUIT-NAME(2)
    MOVE 7 TO FRUIT-QTY(2)
    PERFORM VARYING I FROM 1 BY 1 UNTIL I > 2
        DISPLAY FRUIT-NAME(I) FRUIT-QTY(I)
    END-PERFORM
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: Keep every subscript between `1` and the size of the table. GnuCOBOL does not check this by default, so `TEMP(4)` in a table of three reads or changes memory that belongs to other data items.

card: `05 TEMP PIC 99 OCCURS 3 TIMES.` inside an `01` group
`TEMP(1)` is the first element, `TEMP(I)` element number I
Loop over a table with `PERFORM VARYING I FROM 1 BY 1 UNTIL I > 3`
`01 T VALUE "102030".` fills `05 N PIC 99 OCCURS 3.`
`INITIALIZE T` sets numbers to zero, text to spaces

units.title: Text handling
units.summary: Cut, join, split and change text with reference modification, STRING, UNSTRING, INSPECT and text functions.

lesson.md: Text items have a fixed size and are filled with spaces. COBOL has **intrinsic functions** that help: you write `FUNCTION`, the name and the input in parentheses. `FUNCTION TRIM` removes the spaces at both ends, and `FUNCTION UPPER-CASE` and `FUNCTION LOWER-CASE` change the letters.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. FUNCS.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 CITY PIC X(8) VALUE "Lima".
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    DISPLAY "[" CITY "]"
    DISPLAY "[" FUNCTION TRIM(CITY) "]"
    DISPLAY FUNCTION UPPER-CASE("Lima")
    DISPLAY FUNCTION LOWER-CASE("HELLO")
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: **Reference modification** takes a part of a text: `WORD(start:length)`. `WORD(1:4)` gives the first four characters, `WORD(5:3)` three characters from position `5`. Positions start at `1`. Without a length, as in `WORD(5:)`, you get the rest of the text.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. PARTS.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 WORD PIC X(8) VALUE "COMPUTER".
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    DISPLAY WORD(1:4)
    DISPLAY WORD(5:3)
    DISPLAY WORD(7:)
    MOVE "D" TO WORD(1:1)
    DISPLAY WORD
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: `STRING` joins several pieces `INTO` one item. Each piece has a `DELIMITED BY` phrase: `DELIMITED BY SIZE` takes the whole piece, and `DELIMITED BY SPACE` takes it only up to the first space. `STRING` does not clear the target, so `MOVE SPACES` to it first. `SPACES` stands for as many spaces as the item needs.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. JOIN.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 FIRST-NAME PIC X(10) VALUE "Ada".
01 LAST-NAME PIC X(10) VALUE "Lovelace".
01 FULL-NAME PIC X(25).
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    MOVE SPACES TO FULL-NAME
    STRING FIRST-NAME DELIMITED BY SPACE
        " " DELIMITED BY SIZE
        LAST-NAME DELIMITED BY SPACE
        INTO FULL-NAME
    END-STRING
    DISPLAY "[" FUNCTION TRIM(FULL-NAME) "]"
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: `UNSTRING` does the opposite: it splits a text at a delimiter and puts the parts into several items, from left to right.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. SPLIT.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 DATE-TEXT PIC X(10) VALUE "2024-05-17".
01 YY PIC X(4).
01 MM PIC XX.
01 DD PIC XX.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    UNSTRING DATE-TEXT DELIMITED BY "-"
        INTO YY MM DD
    END-UNSTRING
    DISPLAY "Day " DD " of month " MM " in " YY
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: `INSPECT ... TALLYING N FOR ALL "s"` counts how often `"s"` appears and adds the count to `N`. `INSPECT ... REPLACING ALL "s" BY "z"` replaces every `"s"` with `"z"`. Both texts must have the same length.

lesson.code:
>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
PROGRAM-ID. INSPECT.
DATA DIVISION.
WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
01 WORD PIC X(11) VALUE "mississippi".
01 HITS PIC 99 VALUE 0.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    INSPECT WORD TALLYING HITS FOR ALL "s"
    DISPLAY "Count: " HITS
    INSPECT WORD REPLACING ALL "ss" BY "SS"
    DISPLAY WORD
    STOP RUN.

lesson.md: `TALLYING` adds to the counter and does not reset it. Give the counter the start value `0`, or `MOVE 0` to it before every new count.

card: `FUNCTION TRIM(T)`, `FUNCTION UPPER-CASE(T)`
`T(5:3)` = 3 characters from position 5
`STRING A DELIMITED BY SPACE B DELIMITED BY SIZE INTO C`
`UNSTRING T DELIMITED BY "," INTO A B C`
`INSPECT T TALLYING N FOR ALL "a"` / `REPLACING ALL "a" BY "o"`

01 WORD PIC X(6) VALUE "banana".
INSPECT WORD ___ ALL "a" BY "o"
DISPLAY WORD
exercises.explain: `REPLACING ALL "a" BY "o"` changes every `a` into an `o`.

exercises.prompt: Build the statement that copies CITY up to the first space into OUT-TEXT.
exercises.explain: `DELIMITED BY SPACE` stops at the first space, and `INTO` names the target.

exercises.prompt: Put the lines in order so the code prints 17.05.2024.
exercises.explain: Fill `DATE-TEXT` first, then split it, and print the parts at the end.

exercises.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
Which line has the bug?
exercises.explain: Positions start at `1`, not `0`. Write `WORD(1:3)` for the first three characters.

exercises.prompt: The code should print New York!. Which line has the bug?
exercises.explain: `DELIMITED BY SPACE` stops at the space in `New York`. Use `DELIMITED BY SIZE` to take the whole item.
